changes.new: Результат проекта — обученная модель и воспроизводимый эксперимент, показывающий последствия одного выбранного изменения. ## Worked reference: tracing nanoGPT through an optimizer update With gradient accumulation, several microbatches contribute to one update of the model's parameters. A training script also samples data, evaluates a held-out split, changes the learning rate, writes state, and decides when to stop. Their order determines what a logged loss or saved iteration means. Andrej Karpathy's [nanoGPT, revision 3adf61e1](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/tree/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291) provides a compact working implementation. The source files and quoted excerpts below retain their original English and [MIT notice](/licenses/nanogpt-3adf61e1-MIT.txt). The local packet is `05 Источники/Originals/nanogpt-2026-10-30`. This is a worked reference alongside the assignment above. It does not fill the CS336 adapters or satisfy that assignment's 48 official tests. nanoGPT uses learned positional embeddings, LayerNorm and GELU; the assignment asks for RoPE, RMSNorm and SwiGLU. The shared next-token objective does not make the implementations interchangeable. ### Text becomes a stream of targets The published character preparer builds a sorted alphabet, maps characters to integer IDs, splits the stream 90/10, and writes `train.bin`, `val.bin` and `meta.pkl`. The arrays use `uint16`; the metadata preserves the alphabet and both mappings. This is a character tokenizer, not a BPE tokenizer. Its alphabet is constructed from the whole supplied text before the split, so it should not be described as learning BPE merges on the training split. The loader samples a start index and takes two overlapping windows. For the stream `[0,1,2,3,0,1]`, start 1 and length 3 give input `[1,2,3]` and target `[2,3,0]`. The model receives three known input tokens; the prediction after 3 is supervised by the following 0. Original lines inside [`get_batch`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L123-L125): ```python title="Original nanoGPT excerpt — MIT; surrounding function omitted" ix = torch.randint(len(data) - block_size, (batch_size,)) x = torch.stack([torch.from_numpy((data[i:i+block_size]).astype(np.int64)) for i in ix]) y = torch.stack([torch.from_numpy((data[i+1:i+1+block_size]).astype(np.int64)) for i in ix]) ``` The conversion to `int64` supplies indices for the embedding lookup. In `model.forward(idx, targets)`, logits and targets are flattened at corresponding positions and cross-entropy is computed directly. The loader has already shifted the targets. Applying another shift would train on the token two positions ahead. The [[00 Учебник/11 Pre-training и Scaling/42 Next-token prediction#Реализация без скрытых сдвигов|NTP implementation]] uses a different interface: it accepts one full sequence and performs the shift inside the loss function. For a microbatch with two sequences of eight targets, the loss averages 16 predictions. The source ignores target ID `-1`, not ID 0. In the character fixture below, 0 is a real newline character and contributes to the loss. Changing a tokenizer's ID convention must not silently remove its first vocabulary item from training. ### From microbatches to one update For each accumulation cycle, the script computes a mean loss, divides it by `gradient_accumulation_steps`, and backpropagates. It does not clear the gradients between microbatches. With two microbatches of equal shape `[2,8]`, one update therefore accounts for 32 target tokens. Original update order in [`train.py`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L306-L314): ```python title="Original nanoGPT excerpt — MIT; preceding microbatch loop omitted" # clip the gradient if grad_clip != 0.0: scaler.unscale_(optimizer) torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), grad_clip) # step the optimizer and scaler if training in fp16 scaler.step(optimizer) scaler.update() # flush the gradients as soon as we can, no need for this memory anymore optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True) ``` For scaled FP16 gradients, clipping must operate on unscaled values. The CPU fixture uses FP32 and a disabled scaler, so it checks the update path without testing CUDA mixed precision. With dropout disabled and identical data, its separate FP64 check compares the gradients of a full `[4,8]` batch with two accumulated `[2,8]` microbatches. The largest difference in the recorded run is about `1.25e-16`. That is a numerical check under stated conditions, not a promise of bitwise equivalence for arbitrary stochastic or distributed training. The configuration variable for accumulation is adjusted when DDP starts. The source default 40 is divided by the world size: eight replicas each accumulate five local microbatches. The token count then includes all replicas. Leaving 40 local microbatches on every replica would change the global batch by a factor of eight. This CPU lab does not launch DDP; the collectives and reduction assumptions are developed in [[00 Учебник/11 Pre-training и Scaling/44 Distributed training и mixed precision|distributed training]]. The training-line loss also needs interpretation. After accumulation, the source prints the final microbatch's scaled loss multiplied back by the accumulation count. This recovers that microbatch's mean, not the mean of all microbatches. If their means are 2 and 6, the printed value is 6 while the combined mean is 4. The separate `estimate_loss` routine evaluates multiple random batches in evaluation mode and averages them; it measures another sample of the data at another point in the loop. ### Checkpoint contents and update boundaries Evaluation and saving occur before the current iteration's update. The checkpoint stores the model, optimizer, architecture arguments, iteration number, evaluation value and configuration. It does not store the random-number state, the already prefetched next batch, or the GradScaler state. The native execution below uses `max_iters=2`, evaluation every iteration and `always_save_checkpoint=True`. The ordering is: | Loop label | Completed updates at evaluation | Checkpoint written | Update executed afterwards | |---|---:|---|---:| | 0 | 0 | No: the source requires `iter_num > 0` | First | | 1 | 1 | Weights and optimizer after one update | Second | | 2 | 2 | Weights and optimizer after two updates | Third | After the third update, the counter becomes 3 and the condition `iter_num > max_iters` stops the process. Thus this particular run executes three updates but saves the state after two. With 32 targets per update, the process handles 96 training targets; the saved model has received 64. Validation draws are separate from these counts. This is the behavior of the pinned revision, not a convention that every training framework follows. The second native experiment stops after writing iteration 1, then restarts with `init_from=resume` and continues to a saved iteration 2. Both its checkpoint and the uninterrupted checkpoint contain two AdamW steps, yet their weights differ by up to approximately `0.00172` in this fixture. Restoring parameters and optimizer moments resumes optimization, but the source does not restore the stochastic trajectory or the prefetched input. Matching an iteration label is insufficient to prove exact continuation. A separate resume implementation can save the necessary RNG, scaler and data-loader state at a defined update boundary. Which state is necessary depends on the sampler and distributed layout. The assignment's controlled-continuation criterion above is stronger than merely loading this nanoGPT checkpoint successfully. ### Generation does not use a KV cache in this implementation With targets, the original model returns logits for every position. Without targets, it projects only the last hidden state into the vocabulary: the result has shape `[B,1,V]`. This saves the earlier vocabulary projections, not the Transformer computation for the prefix. The native `generate` method repeatedly runs the full available context, scales its last logits by temperature, applies optional top-k filtering, samples one ID, and appends it. A forward hook in the lab observes input lengths `[6,7,8,8,8]` when five tokens are generated from a six-token prefix with an eight-position context. After the window fills, the source keeps the last eight IDs and recomputes them with positions starting at zero. That is an explicit cropped-context algorithm, not exact KV-cached generation beyond a learned position table. Compare the distinct original OpenAI cache contract in [[00 Учебник/06 Encoder, Decoder и Encoder-Decoder/05 GPT-2 — zero-shot через язык#Сохранение ключей и значений|GPT-2]]. The member named `flash` only tests whether PyTorch exposes `scaled_dot_product_attention`. It does not identify the kernel selected for a particular call. The numerical check forces PyTorch's math backend on CPU while this member is still `True`. Backend selection, dropout and input limitations are documented in [PyTorch SDPA](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.15/generated/torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention.html). No CUDA FlashAttention speedup is measured here. ### Run the complete small reference From the Bookvar repository root, after installing the listed dependencies: ```bash uv run --offline --with torch==2.14.1 --with numpy==2.3.5 \ --with requests==2.32.5 --with tiktoken==0.12.0 \ python '06 Практика/Code/nanogpt_reference_lab.py' \ --output '06 Практика/Results/nanogpt-2026-10-30/reference.json' ``` The script copies the pinned upstream files into a temporary directory and runs them unchanged. It supplies a local 2048-character, four-symbol stream, so the preparer does not fetch Shakespeare. It then runs two fresh training processes, one resumed process, and the original sampling program. The `meta.pkl` route avoids fetching a BPE vocabulary or pretrained weights. Temporary corpora and checkpoints are removed after their contents have been checked. The saved JSON records 1843 training IDs, 205 validation IDs, a 6784-parameter native model, a 110,392-byte temporary checkpoint, and the original program's generated IDs `[2,1,1,1,1]`: the letter `A` followed by four spaces. This output is not evidence of useful language modeling. It checks that text preparation, model construction, optimization, state restoration and sampling are connected. A separate 6832-parameter, seven-token model checks logit shapes, causal-prefix invariance and accumulation gradients. The reported byte count and numerical errors belong to the recorded Python 3.14.3 / PyTorch 2.14.1 run; serialization size and rounding can differ in another environment. The script checks structural and numerical conditions, not those illustrative numbers as a speed or quality threshold. The result does not establish `PASS cpu_local` or `PASS gpu_full` for CS336. ### Reading an actual loss curve ![[00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/nanogpt-2026-10-30/loss-original.png]] *Andrej Karpathy, original [nanoGPT README loss plot](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/assets/gpt2_124M_loss.png). MIT; Copyright (c) 2022 Andrej Karpathy. Entire original PNG, unchanged.* The horizontal axis is labeled Step; the vertical axis is validation loss. The selected logged point is 2.905 at 399. Neither the image nor a milestone such as "learning grammar" identifies what the network learned at one iteration. The plot alone also does not specify enough logging and token accounting to reconstruct a wall-clock training budget from its axis. The README separately reports an OpenWebText reproduction around 2.85. Its unadapted GPT-2 baseline is about 3.12 on OpenWebText; adapting those released weights to OpenWebText also reaches about 2.85. The released model was trained on private WebText, so a comparison on the open replacement includes a domain change. The graph's visible point, the reported final recipe and an independently reproduced benchmark must not be conflated. The README's three-minute character example specifies one A100 run. Its compile and MPS speedups are historical observations, not portable multipliers. A current timing experiment needs its own hardware, software, warmup, synchronization and workload specification. ### nanoGPT, build-nanogpt and nanochat The three repositories serve different purposes. nanoGPT is the implementation traced above. The [build-nanogpt lecture](https://github.com/karpathy/build-nanogpt) constructs a GPT-2 reproduction in a recorded sequence of commits and an accompanying video. The [Zero to Hero GPT lesson](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kCc8FmEb1nY) is another lesson, linked separately in nanoGPT's README. The retained nanoGPT README marks the repository deprecated in November 2025 and points to [nanochat](https://github.com/karpathy/nanochat/tree/92d63d4e8bb4df75c3b71618f31ddde2378b2bcd). The latter's pinned README covers tokenization, pretraining, fine-tuning, evaluation and inference; its GPT-2 speedrun criterion uses a DCLM CORE score rather than simply matching nanoGPT's OpenWebText loss. Costs, hardware, data and evaluation criteria must therefore accompany any "time to GPT-2" comparison. No nanochat training or dollar-cost result has been reproduced by this CPU reference.

## Практика и первоисточники

A worked, executable reference traces the unmodified nanoGPT loader,
optimizer update, checkpoint/resume boundary and sampler in
[[06 Практика/20 Собрать языковую модель с нуля#nanogpt-worked-reference|the nanoGPT practice section]].
It complements the probability and masking derivations above; its CPU
fixture does not reproduce GPT-2 quality or a GPU training benchmark.

## Источники и дальнейшее чтение

For the training path, see
[[06 Практика/20 Собрать языковую модель с нуля#nanogpt-worked-reference|the worked nanoGPT reference]].
Its original sampler recomputes a cropped context without a KV cache;
that behavior is separate from the OpenAI cache contract developed here.
